content.overview: Section 13 provides that two or more persons are said to consent when they agree upon the same thing in the same sense.
content.glance: Consent = agreement upon the same thing in the same sense (consensus ad idem).
content.study: Consent exists when two or more persons agree upon the same thing in the same sense. This is the statutory expression of consensus ad idem. Free consent is defined in s. 14; absence of free consent leads to voidability under ss. 19–19A. Current-law framing: identify the subject-matter; test whether the parties agreed upon the same thing in the same sense; then test freeness under s. 14.

sections.heading: Same thing in the same sense
sections.body: Two or more persons consent when they agree upon the same thing in the same sense.

examples.title: Different subject-matter
examples.body: A intends to sell plot X; B intends to buy plot Y. They have not agreed upon the same thing in the same sense — no consent under s. 13.

hypotheticals.question: Is mere outward agreement enough if the parties mean different things?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 13 requires agreement upon the same thing in the same sense.

distinctions.title: Scope of s-13
distinctions.body: Applies only within the elements and consequences stated in the statutory text.

misconceptions.trap: Any signed document shows consent regardless of mutual understanding.
misconceptions.correction: Section 13 requires agreement upon the same thing in the same sense.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a Section 13 problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the alleged subject-matter. II. Test whether parties agreed upon the same thing in the same sense. III. If yes, test free consent under s. 14. IV. Conclude.

examTips: Quote ‘same thing in the same sense’.
Link to free consent (s. 14) and mistake (s. 20).
